newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian banks, foreign firms strapped for cash.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian banks, foreign firms strapped for cash.

text.p: PHNOM PENH, July 18 (REUTER) - Two weeks after a coup brought Phnom Penh to a bloody halt, Cambodian banks and foreign firms in the capital are desperate for dollars.

The British American Tobacco Company (B.A.T), which employs about 750 people making cigarettes, has less than $2,000 in cash on hand here despite looming tax, wage and vendor obligations of about $500,000.

Dollars are the currency of preference in Cambodia, especially among foreign businesses and aid agencies. Most bank accounts hold dollars rather than riel, the national currency, and all major transactions are in dollars.
"We had some cash when the troubles started but we spent most of it already ," explained B.A.T's finance manager in Phnom Penh, Rithy Chea.
"We have employees and suppliers to pay, but no money. It is very difficult for a large business to operate without the support of banks."
Troops loyal to Second Prime Minister Hun Sen deposed First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh in two days of fighting July 5-6, routing the prince's soldiers.
The coup and several days of looting that followed closed banks and businesses and led to the evacuation of several thousand foreign businessmen, aid workers and their families.

The city is now calm and many businesses have reopened. B.A.T's corporate offices opened on Monday and the production line started up again the next day -- but with only two shifts instead of three because of lingering security fears after dark.
But Banque Indosuez, B.A.T's bank in Phnom Penh, remains closed, forcing the cigarette manufacturer to improvise.

B.A.T officials in Singapore contacted officials from Hotel Sofitel Cambodiana, who are also based in Singapore, and arranged for $10,000 to be made available to B.A.T here through the hotel's account in a local bank that has reopened.
But when the B.A.T finance manager went to withdraw the money on Friday morning, he was told only small withdrawals were being permitted and was asked to return in the afternoon.
"B.A.T managers in Singapore know how important it is for us to have the cash to meet our obligations," Chea said.
"I am 100 percent confident that if, for whatever reason, banks here are unable to supply the money we need, our managers will get it here some other way."
Phnom Penh has about 30 banks. Most are doing business for a few hours every day but are limiting withdrawals to between $1000 and $5000 per customer per day.
Ram Pheuklieng, general manager of the city's Thai-owned Regent Park Hotel, is one of many businessmen here strapped for cash as a result of those limitations.
"Our customers pay with American Express or Visa cards but we have to pay our bills for food and fuel and salaries in cash," the manager said on Friday.

"I need at least $14,000 or $15,000 today but when I went to the bank I was allowed to withdraw only $1,000. Several of us Thai businessmen have asked our ambassador here in Phnom Penh for assistance. We must have access to our own money."
Chea Sok, general director of the National Bank of Cambodia, the country's central bank, acknowledges the liquidity crisis and says he is doing everything he can to correct it.
"I have ordered that all banks be open for business by July 21 at the latest or face substantial fines," Chea Sok told Reuters on Friday.

"We need the banking industry to be operating so we can accept the tax and revenue receipts on which the government depends. Also, it will generate confidence among the people and the big money lenders, who are holding lots of dollars."
But opening the banks won't do much good if they refuse to allow depositors access to their own funds.
"If Banque Indosuez and the Bangkok Bank open on Monday as I expect they will, that should help because they are big banks that handle dollars for large businesses," Chea Sok said.
"In the end it is a matter of confidence spreading. I think there are a lot of dollars here, they just aren't circulating."
